content.title: Logistic Differential Equations
content.overview: Logistic differential equations model population growth that is constrained by a carrying capacity. Unlike exponential growth, which increases without bound, logistic growth accounts for limited resources, causing the growth rate to decrease as the population approaches its maximum sustainable size.
learning_objectives: Identify the differential form of the logistic growth model.
Solve for the growth constant k using observed population values.
Determine the population value where the maximum growth rate occurs.
Apply the closed-form logistic solution to predict future population values.

sections.title: The Logistic Model
sections.content: The logistic differential equation is defined as dP/dt = kP(1 - P/K), where P is the population, t is time, k is the relative growth rate constant (k > 0), and K is the carrying capacity. The term (1 - P/K) represents the fraction of the carrying capacity still available. As P approaches K, the growth rate dP/dt approaches zero. If P starts below K, the population will increase and asymptotically approach K. If P starts above K, the population will decrease toward K.

sections.title: The Closed-Form Solution
sections.content:
The general solution to the logistic differential equation is P(t) = K / (1 + A * e^(-kt)). The constant A is determined by the initial population P(0) = P₀ using the formula A = (K - P₀) / P₀. This solution allows for the calculation of the population at any time t without needing to perform integration repeatedly.

![A sequence of steps to solve for population in a logistic model: Identify K and P0, Calculate A, Solve for k using a second data point, and Evaluate P(t) for the target time.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/2937c605-5b5f-4c1a-b63e-4da86d2a1789-1786519376535-363.webp)

sections.title: Maximum Growth and Inflection Points
sections.content: A critical property of the logistic curve is that the maximum growth rate occurs when the population is exactly half of the carrying capacity (P = K/2). On a graph of P vs. t, this corresponds to the point of inflection where the curve changes from concave up to concave down. To find the maximum rate, substitute P = K/2 into the differential equation: (dP/dt)_max = k(K/2)(1 - (K/2)/K) = kK/4.

worked_examples.question: A population of birds P(t) follows the model dP/dt = kP(1 - P/2000). Initially, P(0) = 400. After 3 years, P(3) = 800. Find the value of k and the instantaneous growth rate when the population is 1000.
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Identify K and A. K = 2000. A = (2000 - 400) / 400 = 1600 / 400 = 4.
Step 2: Use P(3) to solve for k. The solution is P(t) = 2000 / (1 + 4e^(-kt)).
800 = 2000 / (1 + 4e^(-3k))
1 + 4e^(-3k) = 2000 / 800 = 2.5
4e^(-3k) = 1.5
e^(-3k) = 0.375
-3k = ln(0.375)
k = -ln(0.375) / 3 ≈ 0.327 yr⁻¹.
Step 3: Calculate the growth rate at P = 1000. Since 1000 is K/2, this is the maximum growth rate.
dP/dt = 0.327 * 1000 * (1 - 1000/2000) = 0.327 * 1000 * 0.5 = 163.5 birds per year.

common_mistakes: Confusing the logistic model with the exponential model (dP/dt = kP) and failing to include the (1 - P/K) term.
Incorrectly identifying the maximum growth rate as occurring at P = K rather than P = K/2.
Algebraic errors when solving for k, particularly with the signs in the exponent of the closed-form solution.
Forgetting that A = (K - P₀) / P₀ and using P₀ directly in the denominator of the solution.
exam_tips: If a problem asks for the population when growth is fastest, immediately look for K/2.
Always check that your final population P(t) is between the initial value and K; if it exceeds K (when P₀ < K), recheck your k calculation.
Units for dP/dt are always [Population Units] per [Time Units].
The limit of P(t) as t approaches infinity is always K, provided P₀ > 0.
content.recap: Logistic growth is characterized by a rate proportional to both the current population and the remaining capacity. The population P(t) follows an S-shaped curve that levels off at the carrying capacity K, with the steepest growth occurring at P = K/2.

knowledge_claims.content: The logistic differential equation is expressed as dP/dt = kP(1 - P/K), where K is the carrying capacity.
The closed-form solution to the logistic differential equation is P(t) = K / (1 + A * e^(-kt)).
The constant A in the logistic solution is calculated using the initial condition P(0) = P₀ as A = (K - P₀) / P₀.
The maximum growth rate of a logistic population occurs when the population size P is exactly half of the carrying capacity (K/2).
As time t approaches infinity, the population P(t) in a logistic model approaches the carrying capacity K.
The graph of a logistic function P(t) has an inflection point at the coordinates where P = K/2.
It is a mistake to assume the growth rate is highest when the population is closest to the carrying capacity K; the rate actually approaches zero as P approaches K.
To solve for the growth constant k, one must substitute a known population value P(t) at a specific time t into the closed-form solution and isolate k using logarithms.
Unlike exponential growth where dP/dt increases linearly with P, logistic growth dP/dt is a downward-opening parabola with respect to P.
If the initial population P₀ is greater than the carrying capacity K, the population will decrease toward K, and the value of A will be negative.
The term (1 - P/K) in the differential equation represents the percentage of the environment's resources that are still available for population growth.
The maximum instantaneous growth rate in a logistic model is given by the formula (k * K) / 4.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Logistic Differential Equations — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Logistic Differential Equations: Logistic growth includes a carrying capacity, has maximum growth at half that capacity, and approaches equilibrium rather than increasing without bound.
options.B: Vector-Valued Motion: Differentiating a position vector gives velocity, speed is the magnitude of velocity, and acceleration is the velocity derivative.
options.C: Comparison and Limit Comparison Tests: Positive-term series can inherit convergence or divergence from a benchmark through inequalities or a finite positive ratio limit.
options.D: Continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem: Continuity at a point requires an existing limit equal to the function value, and the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees attained values under interval continuity.
